transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-23 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lena (Harbinger Head of ML), Rajiv (CTO), Claire (Infra), Samir (PM)

Summary:
Harbinger is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for an LLM-powered assistant in regulated B2B workflows. Main focus today: per-token unit economics, how batching and KV/prefix caching reduce cost, and fallback/routing policy if we hit capacity. They have a monthly inference budget target and strict latency SLO for key flows. Discussed SOC2/KMS requirements and network residency for an eventual private rollout.

Topics:
- Current stack & request profile
- Budget ceiling and unit cost sensitivity
- Batching, caching, and quantization levers
- Dedicated capacity, burst options, and routing fallbacks
- Compliance (SOC2, KMS, SSO) and on-prem constraints
- Pilot scope and next steps

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros?
[00:12] Lena (Harbinger): Hi, I'm Lena, lead ML. We own the assistant model and prompt sets.
[00:18] Rajiv: Rajiv, CTO, bandwidthed on infra decisions.
[00:24] Maya: Awesome. Ethan, do you want to add?
[00:27] Ethan (Redwood SE): yeah hi - SE on infra and inference runtime, will dive into batching/cache questions.
[00:33] Samir: Samir, PM owning the pilot success criteria.

[02:00] Maya: high level — what's the workload and budget line you're thinking about?
[02:08] Lena: We're prototyping an assistant that backfills product and contract summaries. Roughly 250k requests/day now in test, expected 1M/day in 6 months. Our budget for inference is about $60k/month initially, but want options to cap spend. Latency SLO for priority flows is ~150 to 200 ms p95.

[04:10] Ethan: ok, important constraints. Two levers we'll talk about: batching (amortizes GPU cost across requests) and prefix / KV cache (reuses activations for repeated prefixes). For a high % of repeated prompts, caching can cut token compute massively.
[04:35] Claire: when you say KV cache, is that caching at the token level or whole responses? we have PII concerns so we need to control residency.
[04:46] Ethan: KV caching is internal model KV cache (per-session), not storing raw PII. But we can configure cache TTL and residency; in Hosted we anonymize and rotate caches, in Private you control them behind your VPC.

[06:00] Samir: our product needs occasional long contexts up to 8k tokens. how does that change per-token costs?
[06:09] Ethan: longer sequences increase compute nonlinearly — context length affects memory and kernel selection. For 8k you're looking at higher GPU RAM and slower throughput per GPU. That pushes preferred approach to either dedicated with larger GPUs or heavy quantization and sharding. Batching still helps but sequence length limits batch size.

[07:30] Rajiv: so if we pick Hosted, what's the fallback if Redwood is out of capacity during a surge? we cannot have failures.
[07:38] Maya: good question. Redwood supports policy-based routing: prioritize requests by route or token type, fallback to cheaper/shorter model variants, or route to Dedicated/Private reserved capacity if you have it. We can configure automatic throttles and a degraded-mode response shape.

[09:10] Lena: cost — do you have a per-token ballpark we can use for planning?
[09:15] Maya: for Hosted, typical ranges depend heavily on model and context length. ballpark for a 2k avg seq on a modern open model is $0.0008–$0.002 per token for large encoder-decoder like mixes, but that's very workload dependent. Dedicated committed capacity lowers unit cost — roughly 30–50% lower at scale, because you amortize GPU utilization.
[09:46] Samir: that range is wide. our finance needs a stress-case: worst-case per-token cost times 1M requests/day.
[09:55] Ethan: we'll run a quick calc in the bench and share spreadsheet, but also point out batching and cache can reduce realized cost by up to 3–5x depending on repetition and request size. So worst-case is a planning input but real run rate usually lower after caching/batching optimizations.

[12:00] Claire: what about quantization tradeoffs? we need quality high for legal language.
[12:08] Ethan: quantization to 4-bit or QLoRA-type ops can lower memory and cost, but may introduce a small delta in generation quality. Redwood Optimize gives recommendations per workload; for legal text we often recommend mixed strategy: keep critical intents on FP16 or 8-bit, quantize lower-priority routes. Also can do A/B evals and quality regression alerts tied to test prompts.

[14:20] Rajiv: security checklist — SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs — are all supported?
[14:28] Maya: yes. Hosted has SOC2 plus customer-level audit logs and KMS integrations. Private/VPC offers full KMS/HSM and on-prem options. For SSO we support SAML/Okta and RBAC. We'll send the security pack after the meeting.

[16:45] Lena: curious about burst capacity — we can commit to a baseline but need spikes for new launches.
[16:52] Ethan: Dedicated includes configurable autoscale and burst pools you can reserve; we can set guaranteed baseline throughput and a burst buffer priced separately. Hosted also supports bursting but it's subject to regional availability and may trigger fallback policies.

[19:00] Speaker 3 (background): mm-hmm.

[19:12] Maya: one more note on routing: you can define per-route policies — route high-priority requests to dedicated pool and low-priority to hosted spot pools or cheaper quantized variants. That keeps critical latency paths stable while reducing cost overall.

[21:30] Samir: can we do a hybrid pilot — start Hosted for speed of rollout, then move stable routes to Dedicated?
[21:36] Maya: that's a common path. initial onboarding on Hosted, then dedicated reservation once usage and performance curves are known. Redwood's API and console are consistent across modes to make that migration smooth.

[23:00] Claire: networking — if we run Private behind our VPC, what's the control plane connectivity pattern?
[23:07] Ethan: in Private we ship a customer-managed control plane; provisioning happens over a secured channel you authorise. Data plane stays in your VPC. For on-prem we can support air-gapped installs with offline packaging and HSM integration.

[25:45] Lena: sample prompts — we'll send a distribution sheet. majority are short (<=512 tokens) but 7% are long (>4k).
[25:53] Maya: good, that distribution is exactly what drives cost modelling. If only 7% are long, dedicated routing of those flows to a larger instance and caching for the short ones is efficient.

[27:30] Ethan: about the bench — I'll run three scenarios: Hosted baseline, Dedicated baseline (committed 2x A100-class equivalent), and Hybrid with routing + caching. Each scenario will have latency p50/p95 and per-token cost estimates with batching assumptions (batch sizes 1, 4, 16) and cache hit rates (0, 20, 50%).

[29:15] Rajiv: curious if Redwood exposes cost attribution at token/request level for internal chargeback?
[29:22] Maya: yes — Console shows token-level and route-level cost, you can slice by token type, model, or route and export. We also have tracing hooks for request-level correlates.

[31:40] Samir: can we set hard caps to stop spend? finance needs circuit breakers.
[31:46] Ethan: yes, rate limits and budget-based throttles exist; you can configure per-route quotas that return controlled degraded responses. Also webhooks for budget alerts.

[33:00] Lena: what's typical pilot length and metrics to evaluate?
[33:05] Maya: pilot usually 2–6 weeks: key metrics are cost per useful response, latency SLO adherence, cache hit rate improvement, and regression-free quality on anchor prompts. We'll define an acceptance criteria doc for the pilot.

[35:30] Claire: about audit logs — how long are they retained on Hosted and can we export to our SIEM?
[35:36] Maya: Hosted has default retention 90 days; enterprise plans can extend retention and stream logs to your SIEM via S3/Kinesis connectors. Private you retain as you configure.

[37:20] Rajiv: any gotchas on data residency e.g., EU-only?
[37:26] Ethan: we have region pinning for Hosted, and Private can be deployed into EU infra. For strict residency we recommend Private. We'll include region options in the security pack.

[39:10] Samir: finance will ask for worst-case burn. can you give a realistic stress-case table?
[39:16] Maya: we'll provide one in the pricing sheet: worst-case (no caching, batch=1), mid (20% cache, batch=4), and optimized (50% cache, batch=16) with per-token numbers and monthly totals. That'll help build contingency budgets.

[41:00] Ethan: one technical note — KV cache effectiveness depends on session stickiness and prompt templating. If you have many unique prompts, cache hit drops. For templated legal forms cache helps a lot.

[43:30] Lena: quality tolerance: legal accuracy is top priority. we may accept higher cost for certain routes.
[43:37] Maya: understood — we can help isolate high-sensitivity routes and keep them on higher-fidelity models and FP16. Lower-sensitivity routes can be routed to quantized cheaper variants.

[45:00] Wrap and next steps recap:
[45:05] Maya: recap - Redwood to send pilot pricing and security docs; Ethan bench and spreadsheet due 5/28; Harbinger to send prompt distribution and long-context percent; schedule VPC follow-up.
[45:20] Rajiv: sounds good. we'll sync with finance after the sheet.
[45:27] Lena: thanks all.
[45:30] Maya: thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the infra deep-dive.

End transcript
